name: Jira + GitHub/GitLab integration
summary: The de facto enterprise standard for connecting work items to source control. Jira's native Development field aggregates branches, commits, pull/merge requests, builds, and deployments from connected providers (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, Bamboo) and surfaces them in two places: a compact counter-icon strip on the board card face, and a full Development panel in the work item detail view. State coupling (auto-transition on PR merge, branch creation, etc.) is supported but opt-in via Automation for Jira rules. DoD, structured checklists, and test linkage are deliberately outsourced to dedicated Marketplace apps (Smart Checklist, Checklists for Jira, Xray, Zephyr), which keeps the core surface narrow but fragments the operational picture across vendors.
card_surface: Counter-icon strip rendered as part of the Development field on the card face. Each connected category renders only when at least one item exists: a branch icon with count, a commit icon with count, a pull/merge request icon with count plus a coloured status dot (open green, merged purple, declined red), a build icon (green check / red cross / amber building), and a deployment icon when applicable. Icons are monochrome line glyphs at roughly 12px, the count sits immediately to the right in tabular numerals, and hovering opens a tooltip preview that previews the underlying branch name, PR title, or commit message. Icons only appear if the board contains fewer than 100 work items and the Development field has been explicitly added via Board > Configure > Card layout. There is no branch name on the card face, no PR title, and no reviewer avatars at this level — Jira deliberately compresses to icon+count to keep the card narrow. Empty state: the strip simply does not render; there is no placeholder skeleton or 'no PR' state.
detail_panel: A dedicated 'Development' section in the work item detail view, rendered as a stacked list of typed rows. Row types and order (top to bottom) are: Branches, Commits, Pull requests, Builds, Deployments, Feature flags. Each row collapses to a one-line summary ('2 branches', '14 commits', '1 pull request OPEN') and expands to show the full list. For pull requests, each expanded entry shows PR number, title, source -> target branch, author, current status (Open / Draft / Merged / Declined), provider icon (GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket), and a click-through link to the originating tool. For builds, each entry surfaces the pipeline name, run number, pass/fail icon, and timestamp. Deployments show the environment label (e.g. 'Deployed to staging') and pipeline link. Commits show SHA, message first line, author, and timestamp. The panel is read-only — all editing happens in the source tool. Reviewer state, CI individual check names, and approval counts are NOT first-class in the panel; they live one click away in GitHub/GitLab. [uncertain] Exact row ordering may differ slightly between Jira Cloud and Data Center.
state_coupling: Opt-in via Automation for Jira rules, not on by default. Jira exposes Git events as automation triggers: 'Branch created', 'Commit created', 'Pull request created', 'Pull request merged', 'Pull request declined', 'Build status changed', 'Deployment status changed'. Common configured rules: branch created -> transition to In Progress; PR opened -> transition to In Review; PR merged to main -> transition to Done; build failed -> add a comment and label. Granularity is per-project (each Jira project owns its own automation rules) and conditions can filter on repository, target branch, and PR labels so a rule can fire only for 'merged to main' rather than any merge. State coupling is bi-directional in capability but most teams use it one-way (Git -> Jira). The {{pullRequest.state}} smart value historically returns only Open / Merged / Declined and does NOT expose 'Draft' as a distinct state, which is a long-standing community gap that forces teams to use {{pullRequest.isDraft}} workarounds or pull provider-specific webhooks.
draft_vs_ready_state: Weakly supported. On the card face, the PR icon's coloured status dot only encodes Open / Merged / Declined — a draft PR shows as 'Open' with no visual distinction from a ready-for-review PR. In the detail panel's Pull requests row, GitHub draft PRs do surface a 'Draft' label inline next to the PR title, but it is a text tag rather than a distinct icon or colour. For automation, Jira's pullRequest.state smart value does not return 'Draft' as a state, so teams cannot easily branch automation rules on draft vs ready without webhook workarounds. GitLab merge requests use the 'Draft:' prefix convention, which Jira surfaces as part of the MR title rather than as a separate field. Net effect: a developer scanning a board cannot tell at a glance whether the linked PR is a draft or ready — they must open the panel and read the label.
review_state: Not surfaced on the card face. In the detail panel, reviewer information is collapsed into the PR row as part of the linked PR title and status, but approval counts ('2/2 approved'), blocking review state, and requested reviewer avatars are NOT exposed as first-class fields — they live in the source tool (GitHub/GitLab) and require a click-through to inspect. The Jira Development field treats the PR as an atomic unit: it knows the PR exists and its top-level state, but it does not pull through review-level metadata. Marketplace apps (Git Integration for Jira by BigBrassBand, GitKraken's GIJ) extend this by showing reviewer pills inline in the panel, and some surface approval count as a tooltip, but these are paid add-ons not native to Jira. [uncertain] Native Jira Cloud may have added partial reviewer surfacing in 2024-2025 updates — community discussions reference experimental review-state pills in some Cloud editions.
dod_checklist: Not first-class in core Jira. Jira ships with no native checklist field — Definition of Done is implemented via Marketplace apps, of which Smart Checklist for Jira (TitanApps), Checklists for Jira Pro (HeroCoders), and Issue Checklist are the dominant choices. These apps add a Checklist custom field that supports: reusable templates per issue type, mandatory items that block workflow transitions, status per item (open / in progress / done / skipped / N/A), expandable detail fields, deadlines and mentions, and rich formatting. Completion percentage is exposed as a derived custom field that can render on the card face (e.g. '7/10 DoD') if added to card layout. Smart Checklist integrates with Automation for Jira so templates can be auto-applied on issue creation or transition, and a 'block transition until checklist complete' workflow validator gates state changes. Sub-task based DoD is the budget alternative — teams without a checklist app use sub-tasks as DoD items, which is cheap but pollutes the issue navigator and lacks template support.
test_linkage: Outsourced entirely to Marketplace apps — Jira has no native test management. Xray and Zephyr are the dominant choices, each with different data architectures. Xray stores tests as native Jira work items (Test, Test Set, Test Plan, Test Execution, Pre-Condition), which means every test appears in JQL, the issue navigator, and the Development panel link graph. Zephyr (Scale and Squad) stores tests in its own database with deep Jira UI integration but tests are not Jira issues. On the card face, neither tool surfaces test status by default — a coverage badge or pass/fail count is not part of the standard card layout, though Xray's traceability custom fields can be added (e.g. 'Test Cases', 'Test Coverage') to expose pass-count on the card. In the detail panel, Xray and Zephyr each add a dedicated 'Tests' tab with execution rows showing test name, last result, environment, executor, and timestamp. CI pass/fail (from the Development panel's Builds row) is treated as a separate signal from test management — CI is for unit/integration tests, Xray/Zephyr is for functional/acceptance tests, and there is no native unification of the two.
cicd_status: Surfaced via the Development panel's Builds row and the card-face build icon. Supported providers: Bamboo, Jenkins, CircleCI, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines — Jira receives build webhooks containing the work item key (parsed from commit message or branch name) and aggregates the latest status. Visual treatment: monochrome line glyph (a small 'gear' or 'build' icon) with a status colour (green pass, red fail, amber in-progress). Individual check names are NOT shown on the card face — only an aggregate pass/fail indicator. The Development panel expands to show each build run with pipeline name, run number, status, duration, and click-through. A failing CI run does not automatically appear as a story-level risk signal — Jira shows the red icon but does not generate a discrete risk item; surfacing it as a 'this story is blocked' signal requires an Automation rule (e.g. 'when build status = failed, add label needs-attention').
release_tagging: Fix Version is the canonical Jira release container — a built-in field on every issue type that can hold one or more Version entries scoped to a Jira Project. Versions are first-class objects with name, description, start date, release date, and release status (unreleased / released / archived). On the card face, Fix Version is NOT shown by default but can be added via Board > Configure > Card layout as one of the three custom fields slots. Stories can belong to multiple Fix Versions (it is a multi-select field), which supports backport scenarios. Epics historically could not be assigned to a version directly — only their child stories — though Advanced Roadmaps and Jira Plans now expose epic-level version assignment in Premium tiers. Releases page in Jira shows a version's rolled-up status: total issues, done count, deployment status per environment, and linked PRs. Git tags from GitHub/GitLab are NOT automatically mapped to Fix Versions — they appear as standalone tag entries in the Development panel and require manual or automation-driven mapping to a Version object.
aggregation: Limited and largely absent at the development-data layer. Jira aggregates child story points, status counts, and time tracking up to Epic and parent issues via Advanced Roadmaps / Jira Plans (Premium) and via Automation rules in standard editions — but PR count, branch count, and CI status do NOT roll up to the Feature or Epic card by default. A Feature card with 5 child stories will show its own Development field counters (which only counts branches/PRs/commits linked directly to the Feature's own key, not the children's keys), so in practice Feature cards almost always show empty Development indicators because developers reference story keys, not feature keys, in branch and PR titles. Workarounds: a custom 'Pull request status' rollup field maintained by Automation (sum of children with PR merged), or Marketplace apps (JXL for Jira, Time in Status for Jira) that compute child-aggregated views. The native gap is real and widely complained about — there is no Atlassian-provided '3 of 5 stories have merged PRs' indicator on Feature cards.
environment_deployment_target: Surfaced via the Deployments row in the Development panel and as a deployment icon on the card face when a deployment has occurred. Environments are typed (development, testing, staging, production, or custom) and Jira matches them by name from the connected deployment provider. Visual treatment in the panel: each deployment shows pipeline name, environment label, status icon, and timestamp — most recent environment per pipeline is highlighted. Multiple environments per work item are shown simultaneously in a stacked list, so a single story can show 'Deployed to dev', 'Deployed to staging', and 'Pending in prod' as separate rows. On the Releases page, a Deployments column shows the rolled-up environment status across all stories in the version. The deployment data flows via the Jira Deployment API — providers POST deployment events with the work item key, environment type, state (in_progress / successful / failed / cancelled / rolled_back), and pipeline metadata. Card-face deployment icon shows only the latest non-development environment status as a single colour-coded dot.
traceability_completeness: No native composite traceability indicator. Jira does not ship with a '✓ code · ✓ tests · ✓ DoD · ✓ deploy' progress ring or icon strip on the card or panel. The components exist as separate fields (Development counter strip, DoD checklist completion %, Xray test coverage, Deployment status) but they are not synthesized into a single signal. Teams build this manually with combinations of: custom fields populated by Automation (e.g. a 'Ready for release' boolean that flips when PR merged AND tests pass AND DoD complete), Marketplace apps like JXL or ScriptRunner that compute composite indicators, or workflow validators that gate transitions on multiple conditions. Jira Align (Atlassian's enterprise SAFe tool) does expose a fuller traceability rollup at the feature/epic/portfolio level — including connected code, tests, and deployments — but this is a separate product, not core Jira. The honest assessment: every Jira shop with a traceability dashboard built it themselves. The pattern of a single composite indicator on the card face is a real gap that an EAP prototype could meaningfully fill.
design_pattern: Counter-icon strip on the card face (icon + small count + optional status colour dot per category), expanding to a typed-row Development panel in the detail view. The pattern is consistent across all card types (story, task, bug, feature, epic) — the Development field renders identically wherever it appears. State is encoded in BOTH colour (open green, merged purple, declined red, build green/red/amber) AND in the count number, with text only appearing on hover via tooltip. The icons are monochrome line glyphs to maintain visual quietness and let the status colour do the signaling work. Empty state is implicit absence — the strip simply does not render — which keeps cards clean for non-engineering work items but means there is no 'no code yet' affordance. The strip respects a maximum of around 4-5 visible categories before collapsing to overflow, and the 100-work-item board limit is the most-cited UX complaint (large boards lose the icons entirely). Visually, the pattern is closer to Targetprocess's compact strip than Linear's single-pill compression — Jira chose breadth (show every Git event type) over distillation (one synthesized signal), which is consistent with its enterprise audience but is a cluttered choice by Rams standards.
